stories.topic: Bowling To Rahul Dravid With An Office Cricket Ball
stories.summary: When Ajay was managing editor at Cricket in the mid-1980s, Rahul Dravid visited the office. They played office cricket with a halfway-squeezy/plastic ball that you could give forward or backward spin to make it zip through the air. Ajay's first ball was a wide; Dravid was clean bowled by the next two; Dravid then said 'Fuck you, Shoaib Akhtar, I'm not playing with you' and threw the bat away.
stories.insight: A perfect, self-deflating Ajay anecdote: he sets up a moment of glory (clean-bowling Dravid twice) and immediately undercuts it with the mock-aggrieved 'Shoaib Akhtar' put-down. It also illustrates how a small change in the medium (the trick ball) can dissolve a vast skill gap — context is half of competition.

stories.topic: He Doesn't Know How To Ride A Cycle
stories.summary: Amit confesses that his thought-to-action ratio in cycling is literally zero — he doesn't know how to ride one. He used to be embarrassed about it. Part of it was a privileged childhood (father in the IAS, car always available); part was that once he started working, he lived a public-transport life of local trains and buses in Bombay.
stories.insight: A neat instance of Ajay's earlier line — 'you don't have to be a hen to know about eggs; in fact, being a hen is an impediment to knowing about eggs.' Amit's intellectual passion for cycling is uncoupled from any first-person practice of it, and that detachment may be exactly what lets him see the strategic and tactical structure clearly.

stories.topic: Pogacar's Coup d'Etat And Roglic's Tears (Tour de France 2020)
stories.summary: In COVID-year 2020, veteran Primoz Roglic — former skier whose career began with a horrific junior-championship crash — entered the final time trial of the Tour de France with a comfortable lead and a reputation as Olympic time-trial champion. He didn't bother attacking 21-year-old compatriot Tadej Pogacar in earlier stages because Pogacar was 'only' 30 seconds behind. Pogacar then put in one of the great rides of modern sport, demolishing the time trial and stealing the Tour. Roglic, last to leave because he was in yellow, kept getting radio updates of his teammate-rival's splits; by the final climb you could see tears in his eyes.
stories.insight: Two lessons in one. First, a contender 30 seconds behind on the last decisive day is not 'safely behind' — narrow margins encode the possibility of catastrophic upset. Second, public memory got the story wrong: Roglic finished 5th of 150 in that time trial, a great ride. The narrative 'Roglic collapsed' is false; Pogacar simply ascended. Outcomes are noisy; we should be careful about the stories we read into them.

stories.topic: Sepkuss And The Vuelta Gift That Broke A Team
stories.summary: At the 2023 Vuelta a España, Jumbo-Visma's two stars Roglic and Vingegaard sent their long-time mountain domestique Sepp Kuss into a breakaway as a tactical decoy — to force rival Remco Evenepoel's team to burn energy chasing. Evenepoel collapsed instead, and Kuss ended up in the leader's red jersey with his two superstars sitting 2nd and 3rd. After years of selflessly helping Roglic and Vingegaard win Grand Tours, Kuss was now leading. Social-media outrage demanded the team gift him the win; Vingegaard agreed, Roglic was furious — 'I came here to win.' Roglic ultimately accepted, but left the team afterwards for Bora-Hansgrohe.
stories.insight: Reciprocity within a team has limits — even when justice clearly favours the helper, the star asked to step aside may legitimately feel that the deal he signed up for has changed mid-stream. The episode also shows the new role of the social-media crowd as an external arbiter inside team strategy.

stories.topic: Pogacar's Costly Attack At Col du Galibier (Tour de France 2022)
stories.summary: Defending champion Pogacar (Team UAE) was up against Jumbo-Visma's two-headed monster of Roglic and Vingegaard. The two Jumbo riders attacked him serially — Roglic goes, Pogacar catches; Vingegaard goes from the slipstream, Pogacar catches; Roglic again — until Pogacar said 'fuck it' and tried to drop them all with a pre-emptive attack. He didn't succeed in losing Vingegaard, and burned so much in the attempt that on the final climb of the Col du Granon, Vingegaard rode away from him by three minutes and won the Tour.
stories.insight: When you are alone against two coordinated rivals, every pure-power solution is a trap. Pogacar may also have 'bonked' (run out of calories) — a reminder that elite performance is always shadowed by mundane biology. The deeper teaching: a numerical disadvantage (1 vs. 2) is decisive in sports where slipstream/repeated attack mechanics multiply the defender's costs.

stories.topic: The 2022 Tour Of Flanders — Pogacar Out-Stalled
stories.summary: Pogacar (65 kg, master climber) attacked solo on the climbs and was joined only by 75 kg Mathieu van der Poel — a far better sprinter on the flat. Pogacar knew that if they reached the line together, Van der Poel would beat him in the sprint, so on the run-in he slowed to almost a standstill, refusing to lead and surrender his slipstream. Van der Poel slowed too. While they played cat-and-mouse, three riders from far behind — co-operating because they had nothing to lose — caught up. Van der Poel then won the sprint, Dylan van Baarle was second, Valentin Madouas third, and Pogacar finished fourth.
stories.insight: Game-theoretic stalling can be self-defeating. By optimising for the best-case 1v1, Pogacar created a worst-case scenario in which the alone-against-the-bunch sprint left him last of the four. When you stop racing the clock to play the rider, you give a third party the race.

stories.topic: Lance Armstrong, Floyd Landis And 'Run Like You Stole Something'
stories.summary: On the highest mountain of one of Armstrong's later Tours, his domestique Floyd Landis dragged him up to the front group of four — Armstrong, Landis, Jan Ullrich, Ivan Basso. Armstrong, having already secured his time gains, told Landis 'run like you stole something' — meaning go win the stage, you've earned it. Landis sprinted but the others wouldn't let him go. Armstrong eventually said 'fuck it' and won the stage himself.
stories.insight: A crisp portrait of the leader-domestique contract and its breakdown: Armstrong genuinely tried to gift Landis the win. When the gift failed for tactical reasons, the leader took it back. Loyalty in cycling is real but conditional on the race situation.

stories.topic: Wout Van Aert's Lost Olympic Road Race
stories.summary: In the last Olympic road race, Wout van Aert was the dominant puncher — so powerful that any group he stayed with would lose to him in the sprint. So opponents attacked him serially: any time someone went off, the others would wait, knowing only Van Aert could chase without conceding the race. Eventually Van Aert was tired of chasing; Richard Carapaz attacked, and Van Aert chose not to follow. Nobody else followed either. Carapaz — not a great rider in that company — won gold; Van Aert and Tadej Pogacar split silver and bronze in the chase sprint behind.
stories.insight: When you are clearly the best, the rest can coordinate against you without ever speaking. Strength can be punished by strategy. The lesson generalises: dominant individuals frequently lose to coalitions, especially in repeated games where their relative cost of action is higher than each opponent's.

stories.topic: Wout Van Aert's Heartbreaking Cobble-Classics Bet
stories.summary: Wout van Aert is also a multiple cyclocross world champion, but he skipped the cyclocross world championship one year to do dedicated high-altitude training for the cobbled classics — Tour of Flanders and Paris-Roubaix. He gave up one major championship to optimise for another. At the very first big cobbled monument, Tour of Flanders, he had a terrible crash through no fault of his own and was out for weeks.
stories.insight: Optimal preparation does not buy you outcomes — it only changes the distribution. The bet was correct ex ante; the realisation was cruel. A reminder of how brittle elite athletic careers are to randomness.

stories.topic: Primoz Roglic's Pivot From Skiing To Cycling
stories.summary: Roglic was a teenage Slovenian ski jumper. In a junior world championship around 2007-2008, he had a horrific crash. He recovered enough to ski again but realised he wasn't going to be world-class — perhaps because of a lost developmental phase, perhaps mental scars. So he switched to cycling — late — and became one of the great riders of his generation, winning the Vuelta three times.
stories.insight: Late starts and forced pivots can still produce world-class outcomes when the underlying motor (in his case, sheer competitive drive) is intact. Roglic also exemplifies a recurring theme of bad luck — late entry meant he was sometimes considered a poor bike-handler, and his Tour de France campaigns were repeatedly derailed by crashes, not form.

stories.topic: Greg LeMond Realises The Sport Is Doping
stories.summary: American three-time Tour winner Greg LeMond took a few months off in the late 1980s. When he returned to the peloton he could barely keep up — the pace had become impossibly high in his absence. That, Amit notes, is when he (or another top rider) realised something was deeply wrong: the EPO era had begun. From 1996 onward, an entire generation of Tour winners — Riis, Ullrich, Pantani, Armstrong, Landis — were doping; the federation eventually voided the results entirely rather than redistribute the titles.
stories.insight: Sometimes the cleanest signal that a system is corrupted comes from an honest insider stepping out and stepping back in. The 'baseline' that looks normal from inside is only legible when you compare it to a reference point untouched by the new equilibrium.

stories.topic: Dave Brailsford's Aggregation Of Marginal Gains
stories.summary: Dave Brailsford — the man Jim Ratcliffe of Ineos has now tasked with turning Manchester United around — took over British Cycling and Team Sky in the 2000s. From a programme that 'never won anywhere,' Sky won seven Tours de France in eight years. Brailsford's framework was 'the aggregation of marginal gains': don't look for one big improvement, look for one-percent improvements on every variable — diet, training, position, helmet aerodynamics — and let them compound.
stories.insight: A foundational principle for any complex performance domain. Big breakthroughs rarely come from one heroic intervention; they come from disciplined attention to many small ones that no single observer notices. Amit teaches it to his writing students; Brailsford applied it to bicycles.

core_ideas.concept: You Don't Have To Be A Hen To Know About Eggs
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's framing for the entire episode: Amit doesn't ride a cycle, has never raced one, has zero action time. But that distance is not an obstacle to deep understanding — it can be an asset. 'In fact, being a hen is an impediment to knowing about eggs.' First-person practice locks you into your own corner of the game; the analyst sees the whole board.
core_ideas.quote: You don't have to be a hen to know about eggs. In fact, being a hen is an impediment to knowing about eggs.

core_ideas.concept: Slipstream — The Physics Behind The Strategy
core_ideas.explanation: A cyclist riding directly behind another saves up to 30% of the effort to maintain the same speed, because the lead rider is the one cutting the air. This single fact of fluid dynamics is the seed from which almost every cycling tactic grows: domestiques shielding their leader, breakaway companions rotating turns at the front, sprinters refusing to lead out, the cat-and-mouse stalling at finish lines. A sport that looks like an individual race against the clock is actually a team coordination problem driven by aerodynamics.
core_ideas.quote: All the people that you see on the screen who are cycling are not putting in equal effort. It is the guys who are out on the wind who are putting in that effort and the people behind them are not.

core_ideas.concept: The Three Race Formats — And Their Different Truths
core_ideas.explanation: Single-day stage races (including the five 'monuments'), one-week stage races, and the three Grand Tours (Giro, Tour, Vuelta) demand fundamentally different skills. Single-day races reward explosive punchers and cobble specialists; Grand Tours require an all-rounder who can climb, time-trial, recover for three weeks straight; time trials inside Grand Tours strip out slipstream and become aerodynamics-and-pacing problems. Treat 'cycling' as one sport at your peril.

core_ideas.concept: The Rider Typology — Climbers, Sprinters, Punchers, Domestiques
core_ideas.explanation: Body weight is the master variable. Climbers (60-65 kg) win Grand Tours because power-to-weight matters most up long mountains. Sprinters and punchers (75-78 kg) generate explosive power on flats and short steep climbs but can't survive long ascents. The exception was Lance Armstrong (in the high 70s) — and that, Amit notes, was the doping era, so the exception confirms the rule. Riders who don't excel in any one role become domestiques: workers who sacrifice their own race for a teammate.

core_ideas.concept: The General Classification (GC) Versus The Stage Win
core_ideas.explanation: A Grand Tour gives prizes on totally different metrics. The GC (yellow jersey at the Tour) is total elapsed time over three weeks — what 'winning the Tour' means. Points classification (green jersey) rewards cumulative sprint points; the mountains classification (polka dot) rewards points won at climb summits; white is best young rider. A sprinter willing to lose an hour on a mountain stage to save energy for sprint stages is not failing — he's playing a different game on the same road.

Every road race has a recurring negotiation between a small breakaway and the main pack (peloton). Breakaway riders cooperate to extend their lead despite competing with each other — they rotate turns in the wind because individually they all lose. The peloton calibrates: catch them too early and another break forms, draining your team; catch them too late and they win. Sprinter teams may keep the gap at exactly three minutes, planning the catch for the final 30 km. Sometimes two sprint teams play chicken — 'these fuckers are taking a free roll' — and the breakaway sneaks through.
core_ideas.quote: These fuckers are taking a free roll. They'll have more people at the end. We don't want that to happen.

core_ideas.explanation: Strangers in a breakaway, riders from rival teams, find informal coordination on the fly. Nobody talks (within a team they have radios; between teams they don't). Yet a stable rotation forms because everyone knows that defection — sitting in the slipstream and never pulling — costs the whole effort. Defection is permitted when justified by team logic ('my leader is in the chase'); pure free-riding is 'desperately uncool.' A real-world game-theoretic equilibrium that emerges silently from repeated play.

core_ideas.concept: Numerical Advantage In A Slipstream Sport
core_ideas.explanation: When you have two riders against one in a small group near the finish, you win almost automatically. Rider A attacks; the lone rival has to chase; the moment he catches A, rider B comes out of his slipstream and attacks; rival has to chase again; A re-attacks. Bullets are limited; the lone rival runs out before either teammate does. This is why the Jumbo-Visma duo of Roglic + Vingegaard was such a problem for Pogacar in 2022 — the structure of the game guaranteed asymmetric energy expenditure.

core_ideas.concept: The Sprint Finish — Why Nobody Wants To Lead
core_ideas.explanation: All things equal, the rider in front loses a sprint, because the rider behind comes out of his slipstream at the optimal moment. So at the end of a small breakaway, riders almost grind to a halt, eyeing one another, refusing to lead. This stalling lets larger groups bridge from behind. It's why Pogacar finished fourth at the 2022 Tour of Flanders despite dominating the race: optimising for a 1v1 sprint while the chase pack reformed.

Send your domestique into a breakaway as a tactical poison pill: rivals can't ignore him (he's now on the GC), so they must burn their team's energy chasing. Meanwhile your stars sit comfortably in the peloton conserving theirs. Jumbo-Visma deployed this with Sepp Kuss at the 2023 Vuelta to dismantle Evenepoel's team. The rare side effect: the decoy actually wins the race. Then your team has a moral problem on its hands.

Rather than attacking, dominant teams (US Postal under Armstrong, Team Sky under Brailsford for Froome) used relentless high pace to flatten the race. If your domestiques drive the peloton fast enough, no rival can launch the explosive attack required to escape — the acceleration costs are simply impossible from a high-tempo line. The peloton goes from a triangle to a single string, opponents drop one by one, and your leader arrives at the final climb with teammates still beside him while rivals are alone. Boring, machinic, terrifying — and effective.

Strategy is fixed before the race: who is the team riding for, what stages are we targeting, when do we attack? Tactics are decided in motion, by the director sportif in the team car receiving live data on watts, heart rates, gaps. A well-prepared team has both — a clear strategic plan and the capacity to adapt tactically as breakaways form, weather changes, rivals crash. Cycling is short-term chess inside long-term chess.

'Bonking' is running out of calories mid-race. To prevent it, riders must eat continuously — and a domestique's job often includes dropping back to the team car for bars and drinks, then ferrying them up to the leader. The director sportif over the radio will instruct: eat now. Cycling at the elite level is as much a metabolic management problem as a physical one. Pogacar's catastrophic loss to Vingegaard at Col du Granon may have been a bonk as much as a tactical mistake.

Dave Brailsford's framework, originally for British Cycling and Team Sky: you don't need one big breakthrough. Identify every variable that contributes to performance — diet, training plan, body position on the bike, helmet aerodynamics, sleep, recovery, mechanics — and improve each by 1%. Compounded across dozens of dimensions, the cumulative gain is a different competitive class. It's the mindset that took British Cycling from non-competitor to seven Tour wins in eight years.
core_ideas.quote: You don't need one big improvement. You look at a bunch of different things... improve one percent on each of them, and that aggregation of marginal gains will take you to a whole different place.

core_ideas.concept: The Drug Era And Its Cleansing
core_ideas.explanation: Through the late 1990s and 2000s, professional cycling was systematically doped — EPO providing the equivalent of altitude training, blood transfusions, the works. The federation eventually voided the entire 1996-2010 Tour winners' list rather than redistribute titles, because everyone was on drugs. By the mid-2010s, better policing and the teams' own self-interest cleaned the sport: an athlete's positive test now destroys the team's sponsorship. Speeds remain high but for legitimate reasons — better training, better altitude protocols, better science.

core_ideas.concept: Crashes As The Permanent Floor Of Skill
core_ideas.explanation: A major theme of modern cycling: the best preparation in the world cannot insulate you from the random catastrophe of someone else's wheel touching yours. Roglic, Vingegaard, Evenepoel, Van Aert, Pogacar — all of cycling's recent stars have seen Grand Tour campaigns destroyed by crashes that were not their fault. Cycling at the limits of human performance has a brittle outcome distribution: the better-prepared rider isn't guaranteed to win; he's just more likely to.

core_ideas.concept: Sport As Story, Not Just Spectacle
core_ideas.explanation: We don't just watch sport for the limits of human achievement — we watch for redemption arcs, rivalries, character. Roglic's long search for a Tour, the Pogacar-Vingegaard era, Van Aert vs Van der Poel since their cyclocross youth: these are the narrative threads that make a three-week race a serial drama. Without the stories, the racing is just men on bicycles.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay teases Amit on his cycling expertise: 'You don't look like a guy who would be very fast on a cycle.' Amit: 'This is really a low blow, and the Bengali in me does not appreciate this low blow.'

Ajay's defence of his cricketing record: he was managing editor at Cricket and clean-bowled Rahul Dravid twice in office cricket — but with a trick ball. 'You would not actually see me on a cricket field running around and doing things. I'm Bengali here. Have some peace.'
Dravid's reaction to being clean bowled by Ajay: 'Fuck you, Shoaib Akhtar, I'm not playing with you,' and he threw the bat away.
Ajay on driving in Bombay: 'I am now the best driver in Bombay. Because driving in Bombay is not about driving, it is about Bombay. But that is a subject for another episode.'
Amit on his cycling credentials: 'In cycles, it is literally zero, because I don't know how to ride a cycle.' After Ajay's hen/eggs line, Amit: 'Welcome to our scrambled eggs episode on cycling.'

Amit's parental advisory on the VPN recommendation: 'Just for this reason, I don't want you to get a VPN — young men watching this for porn. Okay, do not do that. It is sinful, save your energy for studying economics and physics and aeronautical engineering.'

Ajay on his juvenile cycling exploits: 'I was good at cycling with both hands off, and riding up a slope with both hands off, riding up a slope and a curve with both hands off.' Amit: 'Had you been French or Belgian, the loss of economics could have been the gain of cycling. You could have been a card-carrying cyclist, Ajayji.'
Chris Horner's signature post-race verdict on bad team tactics: 'Knuckleheads.'

'You don't have to be a hen to know about eggs. In fact, being a hen is an impediment to knowing about eggs.' Ajay's framing for analysis without first-person practice — the underwriting principle for this entire podcast's habit of episodes about sports neither host has played.
Lance Armstrong to Floyd Landis on the final climb: 'Run like you stole something.'
Peloton — the main body of riders. The cycling-equipment brand of the same name takes its name from this term.

The five 'cycling monuments' — Milan-San Remo (La Primavera), Tour of Flanders (Ronde van Vlaanderen), Paris-Roubaix, Liege-Bastogne-Liege, Il Lombardia. The most prestigious one-day races in the sport.
The three Grand Tours — Giro d'Italia, Tour de France, Vuelta a España. Three weeks each, the supreme tests of stage-race cycling.
Director sportif — the team's race director, sitting in the team car, getting TV feeds and live data, calling tactics by radio.
Domestique — French for servant, the cycling term for a team rider whose job is to sacrifice his own race for the leader (carrying drinks, shielding from wind, pacing in the mountains).
Puncheur — French term for a rider with explosive power, capable of short steep climbs and demanding flat efforts. Heavier than pure climbers; more powerful in bursts than sprinters.
